Notes: 62 BCE: Cicero, Pro Flacco 68 (speech of 59 BCE): at Apamea gold collected by the Jews for the Jerusalem Temple and seized by order of the governor L. Valerius Flaccus was weighed in the forum before the praetor - 'auri pondo c paulo minus' (a little under 100 Roman pounds), via the knight Sex. Caesius; c. 20 pounds were seized at Laodicea and smaller sums at Adramyttium and Pergamum. Earliest explicit attestation of Jews at Apamea; implies a large, organized community collecting the Temple tax. Ancient figure is a sum of money, not a head-count: Population blank. [Review fix: Year Established changed from -205 to -62: first explicit attestation (Cicero, Pro Flacco 68, 62 BCE); Zeuxis settling Jews at Apamea c. 205 BCE is an inference]

62 BCE Flaccus seizure, scholarly assessment: Marshall (Phoenix 1975) estimated the c. 100 pounds of gold seized at Apamea as about 135000 drachmae, which 'would give a huge Jewish population if it was the tax for only one year' (half-shekel = 2 drachmae per adult male); Trebilco argues it was more likely the tax of several communities of the Apamean conventus (incl. Acmonia and Eumeneia) and of several years held back during the disturbances in Judea (65-63 BCE), plus voluntary gifts, so 'it remains impossible to estimate the actual population', though 'large Jewish populations were involved, particularly at Apamea'; elsewhere he writes that it 'represents a Jewish population of many thousands in the vicinity of Apamea'. Regional (conventus-wide) inference - Population blank.

62 BCE Flaccus seizure, Ramsay's assessment (Cities and Bishoprics of Phrygia I.2, 1897, ch. XV s.1): Th. Reinach calculated the weight of gold as about 50000 half-shekels (later: over 75000 drachmae), i.e. several years' tax or an extraordinary contribution; Babelon inferred that 'la population d'Apamée à l'époque Romaine était Juive en grande partie'. Ramsay rejects reading the sum as Apamea's own contribution: it 'represented the contributions of large districts', proving only a large Jewish population in Phrygia, though Apameia was 'one of their chief centres' and Jews were far more numerous in the Apamean district than the Laodicean. He also states that before 70 CE the Jews formed a separate self-administering community ('the Nation of the Jews') in Apameia. No resident count: Population blank.

c. 1st c. BCE (midpoint -50): after the Mithridatic Wars (ended 63 BCE) Apamea 'remained a great centre for trade, largely carried on by resident Italians and by Jews' (Wikipedia, drawing on D.G. Hogarth, Encyclopaedia Britannica 1911, s.v. Apamea 2). Presence of a Jewish merchant community; no count. Wikipedia used as last resort.

c. turn of the era (Collins' range 30 BCE-70 CE; year 1 used as approximate midpoint): Jewish substratum of Sibylline Oracles Books 1-2 (1.1-323, 2.6-33), which places 'Ararat' and the resting-place of Noah's Ark at the springs of the Marsyas, i.e. just behind Apamea (Sib. Or. 1.261-267); Trebilco follows the 'general agreement' that it was written in Phrygia, probably at Apamea, and calls it 'the only document to have survived from Jews in Asia Minor in this period'. Indicates a literate Hellenized Jewish community engaging the city's local flood tradition. Later evidence (the city's Noah/NOE coins of late 2nd-3rd c. CE; 3rd c. CE 'law of the Jews' tomb inscription) is outside the period.
